flawed_step: The claim that greedy coloring uses at most chi(G)+1 colors in every vertex order is false. For some orders, greedy can use far more colors than chi(G)+1.
counterexample: Take the crown graph G = K_{4,4} minus a perfect matching. Its vertices are a1..a4 and b1..b4, with ai adjacent to bj exactly when i≠j. G is bipartite and has edges, so chi(G)=2 and chi(G)+1=3. Process the vertices in the order a1,b1,a2,b2,a3,b3,a4,b4. a1 gets 1. b1 gets 1, since it is not adjacent to a1. a2 gets 2, since its colored neighbor b1 has 1. b2 gets 2, since its colored neighbor a1 has 1. a3 gets 3, since b1 and b2 have 1 and 2. b3 gets 3, since a1 and a2 have 1 and 2. a4 gets 4, since b1, b2 and b3 have 1, 2 and 3. b4 gets 4, since a1, a2 and a3 have 1, 2 and 3. Greedy uses 4 colors, and 4 > 3 = chi(G)+1.
assessment_summary: The statement is false. On the crown graph K_{4,4} minus a perfect matching (chromatic number 2), the order a1,b1,a2,b2,... makes greedy use 4 colors, which is more than chi+1=3. I checked this step by step. In general, K_{n,n} minus a perfect matching makes greedy use n colors.
